channel.title: Ajahn Funn Ācāro Quotes
channel.description: Dhamma quotes by Ajahn Funn Ācāro, updated every 24 hours

item.title: Ajahn Funn: So, what is the mind like? There is the mind of a villain, the mind of a prisoner. There is the mind that…
item.description:
The Mind Can Be Anything: Villain, Prisoner, Animal, Ghost, Indra, Brahmā

So, what is the mind like? There is the mind of a villain, the mind of a prisoner. There is the mind that is miserable and poor. There is the mind of an animal, the mind of a ghost or a hell-being. There is the mind of Indra or Brahmā, the mind of a great king or emperor, the mind of a wealthy millionaire, the mind of a beautiful person, a rich and fortunate person, someone who is neither poor nor suffering. There is the mind of a military officer, a general, a field marshal. The mind can be any of these. What can you say? Choose for yourself. You have come here – what do you want? The Dhamma is like this. The Buddha taught about our refuge. We have ordained, we have listened. In our ordination we received the precepts, and he told us what our refuge is. He didn’t say anything else. He didn’t say, “Possessions, money, and gold – saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.” “Parents and siblings – saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.” “Buildings and houses – saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.” No one ever takes refuge in that way, right? There is only “Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi” – that’s it, isn’t it? Then “dutiyampi” – the second time, “tatiyampi” – the third time, “saraṇa-gamanaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ” – finished. This is our refuge. Apart from this, there is none.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: To move even closer in: “These eyes are mine, these ears are mine, this nose is mine, this tongue is mine, this body…
item.description:
If These Things Really Were Yours, Would You Have Them Go Bleary or Deaf?

To move even closer in: “These eyes are mine, these ears are mine, this nose is mine, this tongue is mine, this body is mine, this mind is mine”—but none of it’s true. How could it be yours? How can you depend on any of these things for long? You can’t even take your body with you. If these things really were yours, would you have your eyes go bleary? Would you have your ears go deaf? Your nose. Your body: Would you have it be in pain? Would you have it get too hot or too cold? If it really were yours, you wouldn’t do any of these things. So contemplate this. Don’t be deluded and infatuated. This body is the body of Māra—the Māras of the aggregates.

The Māras of the aggregates aren’t anything else: They’re form, feelings, perceptions, fabrications, consciousness. These are the Māras of the aggregates. Form is your body sitting right here. Feelings are feelings of pleasure or pain. Perceptions are labels and meanings. Fabrications are thoughts you put together. Consciousness is awareness. All of these things are Māras.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Likewise, if our mind gets lost and turns toward attraction but doesn't get what it wants, we suffer. If it turns toward aversion,…
item.description:
Whatever Arises, Know It but Don't Cling – The Knower Is in the Middle of the Chest

Likewise, if our mind gets lost and turns toward attraction but doesn't get what it wants, we suffer. If it turns toward aversion, not wanting to see or hear something, but then sees or hears it anyway, we suffer, don't we? So we must not turn off. Walk the middle way. Whatever arises, know it, but don't cling to it.

Buddho, the knower, is right here in the middle of our chest. From now on, you should all come to know and see this. This is the practice, the conduct that reaches Dhamma, reaches Vinaya, reaches the religion. Know and reach your own body and mind. Right now, we don't reach our body. We don't reach our mind. Our mind floats off after sense objects: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects. It feeds on external objects. But when it reaches our body, it sees happiness and suffering. Why is there happiness? Because our mind is calm, still, equanimous – not sending itself forward, backward, left, right, up, or down. It stays fixed in the middle, right at that knowing. This mind is not something that is inherently suffering or difficult. It has been this way from the very beginning. But we mix all sorts of things into it, and so it becomes all sorts of things. Therefore, the Buddha taught us to let go.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: See? Sitting here, your mind is still suffering — heavy, sluggish, drowsy, dull, miserable. It torments body and self, pain here, ache there.…
item.description:
Kamma Arises from Body, Speech, and Heart – Mental Kamma Is the Inclining of Mind

See? Sitting here, your mind is still suffering — heavy, sluggish, drowsy, dull, miserable. It torments body and self, pain here, ache there. It gives rise to diseases, dangers, defilements, nuisances, evil and depravity, misery and hardship. This is vipassanā. We know clearly and see truly. The truths (sacca-dhamma) do not come from elsewhere. Quickly recollect Buddho to cut it off. Do not leave it. If we leave it, we will continue to be poor, suffering people, continue to be evil and depraved. We don't want these things, do we? So see: when the mind is not good, that is suffering. Contemplate until it is certain. This is what we call kamma — that or this. Where does kamma come from? Kamma does not come from the sky, air, trees, mountains, or hills. Kamma by body (kāya-kamma), kamma by speech (vacī-kamma), kamma by mind (mano-kamma) — kamma arises from our body, from our speech, from our heart.

So kamma arises from this. At this moment, our bodily kamma is already good, our verbal kamma is already gone. Only mental kamma remains — the inclining of mind. Whatever kamma we incline toward, whether good kamma or bad kamma. Kammassako mhi — I am the owner of my kamma.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: We have come to do merit – have we gained merit? Look. This mind of ours is the Buddha – the knower. Let…
item.description:
Happiness Is None Other Than Our Mind Being Happy; Ease Is the Mind Being at Ease

We have come to do merit – have we gained merit? Look. This mind of ours is the Buddha – the knower. Let everyone determine: know where the knower is, then set mindfulness there. Gaze there. When the mind becomes calm and good, happy and at ease, cool-hearted, free from suffering, heat, turmoil, and trouble – this brings happiness and prosperity in the present and in the future. Look at your mind like this. We came here wanting happiness and prosperity, wanting ease and comfort. It is like this. The reason is none other: happiness is none other than our mind being happy; ease is none other than our mind being at ease. Listen. Listen to know, listen to understand, all of you. This is how it is.

What is unwholesome? It is that the mind is not calm, the mind is not good. When the mind is not good, it becomes miserable, troubled, turbulent, and distressed. This leads beings to fall into suffering and poverty in the present and in the future. Let everyone investigate. Some people suffer losses, become bankrupt, fall into debt – why? Some people work and don’t succeed, seek things and don’t get them – why? Look. Where is it not good? This is how people are.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Now, contemplate the abyākata dhamma (the indeterminate, or that which is not subject to classification). It is not happiness, not suffering. It does…
item.description:
Abyākata Dhamma – Indeterminate: Equanimity, Letting Go, Single Object of Mind

Now, contemplate the abyākata dhamma (the indeterminate, or that which is not subject to classification). It is not happiness, not suffering. It does not grasp at happiness, does not grasp at suffering. Upekkhā — equanimity, letting go. It does not reach out forward or backward. It does not conceive high or low, near or far, inside or outside. It does not signify "this" or "that." Buddho — the knowing, individually present as one thing — is ekaggatārammaṇa, a single object of mind. This is the abyākata dhamma — the indeterminate. It does not conceive or assume, does not conceive cool or hot, dark or light, or any of these conventional designations. It does not conventionally designate "this" or "that." Vimutti — freedom, complete release. That is the crucial point.

Therefore, let us all focus and observe. Each person focus and look: our heart — what is it? What is stuck in it? Investigate. Is it dark or bright? Yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ — knowledge and vision of things as they really are. The reality of our own existence: however it is, let us focus and see. If it is ambitious, grasping at forms, tastes, smells, sounds, tactile objects, mental phenomena — external sense bases — then we investigate birth, aging, sickness, and death. Do we like that birth? Do we like that aging? Do we like that sickness and disease? Do we like that death? Are we delighted by it? If not, then why do we grasp at this and that, creating causes here and there?

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Now, we want to know what our self is like, what our refuge and our abode are like. We want to know. How…
item.description:
What Being Good Is Like: Mind Calm, Joyful, Bright – No Suffering, No Heat

Now, we want to know what our self is like, what our refuge and our abode are like. We want to know. How is it? Is it happy or suffering? Is it good or bad? Measure and find out. Wherever the knowing is, set mindfulness there. The eyes focus there. Our ears listen there. Why listen? Because we want to know whether we are good or bad, happy or suffering. What is being good like? Our mind is calm, our mind is good, has happiness and ease, cool in body and cool in heart, no suffering, no heat, no turmoil, no chaos. Buddho — the mind is joyful, bright in the chest and heart. See? That is what being good is like. Good like this brings happiness and progress in the present and in the future.

We came here wanting happiness and ease. This is the matter. Our mind is at ease as just explained. Know that our mind drinks in happiness and ease, cool in body and cool in heart, no suffering, no heat, no turmoil, no chaos. This very Dhamma element brings our refuge. This is our abode. This very Dhamma element protects a person, leading them to a good destination (sugati) in the present and the future. This Dhamma element brings happiness and progress.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: Is it really a person? If you see that it’s a person, then why do you complain about its aches and pains? Why…
item.description:
If You Want to Solve These Problems, Hurry Up and Solve Them Now

Is it really a person? If you see that it’s a person, then why do you complain about its aches and pains? Why do you complain about its being tired or hungry? Why do you complain about the suffering and difficulties it puts you through? Why is there nothing but hardship and irritation around it? Why is it like that? Everyone who comes here has diseases and dangers, this or that symptom—no worse than I am these days. This person has stomachaches, earaches, headaches, pains in the intestines, pains in the back, pains in the shins, pains in the thighs, pains in the eyes. That person says, “Ohh, I’ve lost money, I’m in debt…” So why is it like that? Look to see how it’s come about. People complain—everyone who comes. This person suffers from this; that person suffers from that.

If you want to solve these problems, hurry up and solve them now. Who else can you have solve them for you? You have to solve them yourself. Even the Buddha couldn’t take them away for you. If he could have, he would have taken them away into unbinding with him. He was able only to point out the path of practice—in other words, right now.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: The scriptures say nothing far away. What they say is: pañcakkhandhā — rūpakkhandha, vedanākkhandha, saññākkhandha, saṅkhārakkhandha, viññāṇakkhandha. This is the Dhamma. Take yourselves…
item.description:
The Five Aggregates Are Within Yourself – Heaps of Merit, Evil, Heaven, Nibbāna

The scriptures say nothing far away. What they say is: pañcakkhandhā — rūpakkhandha, vedanākkhandha, saññākkhandha, saṅkhārakkhandha, viññāṇakkhandha. This is the Dhamma. Take yourselves as the Dhamma. The Buddha's teachings are all within yourselves.

Pañcakkhandhā — the five aggregates. Khandha means group, heap. The heap of form, heap of feeling, heap of perception, heap of formations, heap of consciousness — all these heaps are within yourselves. The heap of merit, the heap of evil are all here. The heap of heaven, the heap of Nibbāna are all within yourselves. Do not think of anywhere else. The heap of happiness and the heap of suffering are all within yourselves.

Therefore, you should all know clearly. This is the Abhidhamma. That is why they say the Dhamma is within yourselves. Rūpa is physical phenomenon, nāma is mental phenomenon. How could it belong to the Buddha? The Buddha taught us to know ourselves. It is just mano — that is, respect. Wherever you incline with respect, you go accordingly.

item.title: Ajahn Funn: To summarize things here in the present: Our body is good and quiet—happy and at ease. The heart is at peace—free from suffering…
item.description:
There Is No Happiness Aside from the Quiet Mind

To summarize things here in the present: Our body is good and quiet—happy and at ease. The heart is at peace—free from suffering and trouble. Unperturbed. Kāya-lahutā; citta-lahutā. Lahu, light. The body is light; the mind is light. With this kind of lightness, everything’s light. Your work is light. Everything’s light. That’s how it is.

This is why I have you focus on watching these things so that you can know and see. We want happiness and ease, but nothing else is happiness and ease aside from a mind that’s quiet. In the Canon, the Buddha says, N’atthi santi paraṁ sukhaṁ: There is no happiness aside from the quiet mind. So focus on in. No happiness aside from a quiet mind. This quietness is happiness, right here and now. Outside as well as in. If what’s inside isn’t quiet, how can what’s outside be quiet?
